summary: The ForCES architecture separates control from packet forwarding. This standards-track RFC applies the same modeling approach to management of the Forwarding Element itself, by defining a Logical Functional Block that represents the Forwarding Element Manager. It lets resources beyond plain packet forwarding be managed in the same way.

eli5.summary: A big machine has a part that does the work and a part that manages it. This describes a way to treat the manager as just another piece you can control with the same tools.

subtitle: A ForCES building block that lets a control element configure the forwarding element itself: its CEs, its LFB classes and its debug logging.

tldr.problem: In a ForCES network element, the forwarding element (FE) also needs runtime configuration, such as which control elements to connect to, which new LFB classes to load and how verbose its debug logging is. Without a standard way to express that, each implementation would invent its own.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the Subsidiary Mechanism (SM) LFB class, with four tables (Debug, LFBLoad, AttributeValues, CEs), three capabilities and four events, so that a CE can change an FE's configuration using ordinary ForCES messages.
tldr.outcome: The SM LFB was registered as LFB class 19, version 1.0. It does not standardize the FE Manager interface (Ff) and leaves LFB-loading parameters and attribute names to implementations.

today: RFC 7729 is a Proposed Standard, published in December 2015, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It leaves the parameters for LFB loading and the attribute names for a future document.

sections.title: Why Manage the Forwarding Element
sections.content:
The Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) architecture splits a network element into Control Elements (CEs) and Forwarding Elements (FEs). The RFC says deployment experience has shown that ForCES is also useful for managing resources other than packet forwarding.

Following that idea, the work of the Forwarding Element Manager (FEM) is modeled as a Logical Functional Block (LFB) called the Subsidiary Mechanism (SM) LFB. A CE that controls an FE's resources can then also manage the FE's configuration through the SM LFB. On a running FE, a CE application may update the runtime configuration through an SM LFB instance.

The RFC is careful about scope. It assumes the FEs are already booted. It does not specify or standardize the FEM-FE interface (called Ff in the ForCES framework); the SM LFB describes only a subset of the operations that can be done over Ff and does not suggest moving away from it. It also makes no assumption about whether FE resources are physical or virtual.
sections.eli5: The part of the machine that moves things around can now also be told how to behave while it is running. The new control panel does not replace the old manager, it just covers a few of its jobs.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
All the use cases assume an FE is already booted and tied to at least one CE. Adding a CE to the FE's table of CEs makes the FE set up a ForCES association with it. Deleting a CE from the table makes the FE end its connection with that CE.

  • High availability: for redundancy, a management application asks an FE to also associate with a backup CE. It supplies the new CE's Control Element ID (CEID), which must be unique within the network element, and its IPv4 or IPv6 address.
  • Scalability: if a CE becomes a bottleneck, a new CE can be booted and some FEs moved to it. The FE is first asked to connect to the new CE, then told to change its master, as described in RFC 7121.
  • Adding resources: an FE in a resource pool can be moved to a working network element by asking it to connect to a CE there and then to disconnect from the pool's CE.
  • New LFB class installation: a CE reads the DynamicLFBLoading capability to learn whether the FE can load new LFB classes, and if so asks it to load one.
  • Logging: a CE may need to raise or lower debug levels for parts of the FE, called modules. The levels come from the syslog message severities registry defined by RFC 3164.
  • General-purpose attributes: a generic name-value table can hold configuration data. The RFC's example is a data-center switch with identical LFBs that can act either as a Spine or a Top-of-Rack switch, with an attribute telling it which role to play.
sections.eli5: The control panel lets the boss add a backup helper, move a worker to a busier team, install a new tool, turn the diary detail up or down, and leave sticky notes such as "you are the front-door switch today".

sections.title: Where an SM LFB Instance Lives
sections.content:
The applicability statement gives two example scenarios. They are not implementation requirements; they show how the SM class can be used.

  • FE integrated: only one instance of the SM LFB class exists and it is directly tied to the FE.
  • Virtual FEs: when the FE software has hierarchical virtual FEs, multiple SM LFB instances can exist, one per virtual FE. In that case the individual FE managers can control the creation, configuration and resource assignment of virtual FEs inside a physical FE.
sections.eli5: A real machine has one control panel. If it is secretly several pretend machines in one box, each pretend machine gets its own panel.

sections.title: Data Types in the SM Library
sections.content:
The SM library defines no frames and no metadata, and the SM LFB handles no packets. It defines five data types:

  • loglevels: an enumerated char-based type of debug levels, derived from syslog.
  • LogRowType: a struct with the module name (lmodule, string), an optional file name and an optional debug level.
  • CERow: a struct with the address family of the CE's IP (uchar, 2 for IPv4 and 10 for IPv6), the CE's IP in an octetstring[16], and an optional CE ID (uint32).
  • LCRowtype: a struct with the LFB class ID (uint32), and optional version (string[8] in the table, string in the XML), name and parameters.
  • NameVal: a struct with an attribute name and an attribute value, both strings.

The log level values run from DEB_OFF (-1, logging off) through DEB_EMERG (0) to DEB_DEBUG (7).
sections.eli5: These are the forms the boss fills in: one for a diary setting, one for a helper's address, one for a tool to install, and one for a free-form sticky note.

sections.title: The SM LFB: Components, Capabilities and Events
sections.content:
The SM LFB (LFB class ID 19, version 1.0) has four components, three capabilities and four events. Its XML definition is given in the RFC.

Components:

  • Debug (ID 1, read-write): a table of modules and debug levels. Changing a row changes the debug level of that module.
  • LFBLoad (ID 2, write-only): a table of LFB classes the FE loads. Adding a row asks the FE to load a class; removing a row unloads it when possible. This changes the SupportedLFBs capability of the FEObject LFB. Each row MUST give the LFB class ID. The version is optional, and the FE MUST assume version 1.0 when it is not given.
  • AttributeValues (ID 3, read-write): the generic name-value table.
  • CEs (ID 4, write-only): the CEs the FE should be able to connect to. Adding a row asks the FE to connect; deleting one asks it to end the connection.

Capabilities: DynamicLFBLoading says whether the FE can load LFB classes dynamically. SupportedParameters and SupportedAttributes are placeholders that will list supported LFB-loading parameters and attribute names. The RFC standardizes none of these yet and expects a future document to do so.

Events: CEAdded and CEDeleted report a CE row being added or deleted, and LFBLoaded and LFBUnloaded report the same for the LFBLoad table. Each event report carries the added or deleted row contents.

Because attribute values, LFB-load parameters and module information are strings, a CE can find the size limits from the component properties defined in RFC 5812.
sections.eli5: The panel has four drawers (log settings, tools to install, sticky notes, helper list), a few signs saying what the machine can do, and a bell that rings whenever something is added or removed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not alter the ForCES model (RFC 5812) or the ForCES protocol (RFC 5810), so it claims no impact on their security considerations.

On trust, the entity that creates new CE connections is either the FE manager responsible for the FEs or an already associated CE. That entity is assumed to be trusted already. If it is faulty, rogue or hacked, the FE cannot tell and will perform any action the CE requests. The RFC therefore does not try to analyze misuse of the SM LFB, and leaves that, with mitigations, to designers of a particular SM implementation. It points readers to Section 8 of the ForCES framework, RFC 3746, for the threat analysis.
sections.eli5: The machine obeys whoever it already trusts. If that boss turns out to be a bad one, the machine cannot tell, so choosing who may use the panel matters.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC registers one entry in the "Logical Functional Block (LFB) Class Names and Class Identifiers" registry: LFB class identifier 19, name SM, version 1.0, described as an SM LFB to standardize subsidiary management for ForCES Network Elements. The registration procedure is Standards Action for identifiers 0 to 65535 and First Come First Served, with any publicly available specification, for identifiers over 65535.
sections.eli5: The panel gets its own official number, 19, in the list of every kind of block so nobody else uses it.
